chunks.citation: RA 9344 (Juvenile Justice and Welfare Act of 2006), Title/Preamble
chunks.text:
REPUBLIC ACT NO. 9344 — JUVENILE JUSTICE AND WELFARE ACT OF 2006
AN ACT ESTABLISHING A COMPREHENSIVE JUVENILE JUSTICE AND WELFARE SYSTEM, CREATING THE JUVENILE JUSTICE AND WELFARE COUNCIL UNDER THE DEPARTMENT OF JUSTICE, APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
Approved: April 28, 2006
(Note: several sections below were later amended by RA 10630, 2013 — see ra10630.txt for the amended versions. Where the two differ, RA 10630's version controls.)

chunks.citation: RA 9344 (Juvenile Justice and Welfare Act of 2006), Sec. 1
chunks.text: SEC. 1. Short Title and Scope. - This Act shall be known as the "Juvenile Justice and Welfare Act of 2006." It shall cover the different stages involving children at risk and children in conflict with the law from prevention to rehabilitation and reintegration.

chunks.citation: RA 9344 (Juvenile Justice and Welfare Act of 2006), Sec. 2
chunks.text:
SEC. 2. Declaration of State Policy. - The following State policies shall be observed at all times:
(a) The State recognizes the vital role of children and youth in nation building and shall promote and protect their physical, moral, spiritual, intellectual and social well-being. It shall inculcate in the youth patriotism and nationalism, and encourage their involvement in public and civic affairs.
(b) The State shall protect the best interests of the child through measures that will ensure the observance of international standards of child protection, especially those to which the Philippines is a party. Proceedings before any authority shall be conducted in the best interest of the child and in a manner which allows the child to participate and to express himself/herself freely.
(c) The State likewise recognizes the right of children to assistance, including proper care and nutrition, and special protection from all forms of neglect, abuse, cruelty and exploitation, and other conditions prejudicial to their development.
(d) Pursuant to Article 40 of the United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child, the State recognizes the right of every child alleged as, accused of, adjudged, or recognized as having infringed the penal law to be treated in a manner consistent with the promotion of the child's sense of dignity and worth, taking into account the child's age and desirability of promoting his/her reintegration.
(e) The administration of the juvenile justice and welfare system shall take into consideration the cultural and religious perspectives of the Filipino people, particularly the indigenous peoples and the Muslims, consistent with the protection of the rights of children belonging to these communities.
(f) The State shall apply the principles of restorative justice in all its laws, policies and programs applicable to children in conflict with the law.

chunks.citation: RA 9344 (Juvenile Justice and Welfare Act of 2006), Sec. 3
chunks.text: SEC. 3. Liberal Construction of this Act. - In case of doubt, the interpretation of any of the provisions of this Act, including its implementing rules and regulations (IRRs), shall be construed liberally in favor of the child in conflict with the law.

chunks.citation: RA 9344 (Juvenile Justice and Welfare Act of 2006), Sec. 4
chunks.text:
SEC. 4. Definition of Terms. - The following terms as used in this Act shall be defined as follows:
(a) "Bail" refers to the security given for the release of the person in custody of the law, furnished by him/her or a bondsman, to guarantee his/her appearance before any court.
(b) "Best Interest of the Child" refers to the totality of the circumstances and conditions which are most congenial to the survival, protection and feelings of security of the child and most encouraging to the child's physical, psychological and emotional development.
(c) "Child" refers to a person under the age of eighteen (18) years.
(d) "Child at Risk" refers to a child who is vulnerable to and at the risk of committing criminal offenses because of personal, family and social circumstances, such as: (1) being abused; (2) being exploited; (3) being abandoned or neglected; (4) coming from a dysfunctional or broken family; (5) being out of school; (6) being a streetchild; (7) being a member of a gang; (8) living in a community with a high level of criminality or drug abuse; and (9) living in situations of armed conflict.
(e) "Child in Conflict with the Law" refers to a child who is alleged as, accused of, or adjudged as, having committed an offense under Philippine laws.
(f) "Community-based Programs" refers to programs provided in a community setting developed for purposes of intervention and diversion, as well as rehabilitation of the child in conflict with the law, for reintegration into his/her family and/or community.
(g) "Court" refers to a family court or, in places where there are no family courts, any regional trial court.
(h) "Deprivation of Liberty" refers to any form of detention or imprisonment, or the placement of a child in conflict with the law in a public or private custodial setting.
(i) "Diversion" refers to an alternative, child-appropriate process of determining the responsibility and treatment of a child in conflict with the law on the basis of his/her social, cultural, economic, psychological or educational background without resorting to formal court proceedings.
(j) "Diversion Program" refers to the program that the child in conflict with the law is required to undergo after he/she is found responsible for an offense without resorting to formal court proceedings.
(k) "Initial Contact With the Child" refers to the apprehension or taking into custody of a child in conflict with the law by law enforcement officers or private citizens.
(l) "Intervention" refers to a series of activities which are designed to address issues that caused the child to commit an offense. It may include counseling, skills training, education, and other activities.
(m) "Juvenile Justice and Welfare System" refers to a system dealing with children at risk and children in conflict with the law, which provides child-appropriate proceedings, including programs and services for prevention, diversion, rehabilitation, re-integration and aftercare.
(n) "Law Enforcement Officer" refers to the person in authority or his/her agent as defined in Article 152 of the Revised Penal Code, including a barangay tanod.
(o) "Offense" refers to any act or omission whether punishable under special laws or the Revised Penal Code, as amended.
(p) "Recognizance" refers to an undertaking in lieu of a bond assumed by a parent or custodian who shall be responsible for the appearance in court of the child in conflict with the law.
(q) "Restorative Justice" refers to a principle which requires a process of resolving conflicts with the maximum involvement of the victim, the offender and the community.
(r) "Status Offenses" refers to offenses which discriminate only against a child, while an adult does not suffer any penalty for committing similar acts, e.g. curfew violations, truancy, parental disobedience.
(s) "Youth Detention Home" refers to a 24-hour child-caring institution managed by accredited LGUs and licensed/accredited NGOs providing short-term residential care for children in conflict with the law awaiting court disposition.
(t) "Youth Rehabilitation Center" refers to a 24-hour residential care facility managed by DSWD, LGUs, or licensed/accredited NGOs, which provides care, treatment and rehabilitation services for children in conflict with the law.
(u) "Victimless Crimes" refers to offenses where there is no private offended party.

chunks.citation: RA 9344 (Juvenile Justice and Welfare Act of 2006), Sec. 5
RA 9344 (Juvenile Justice and Welfare Act of 2006), Sec. 6
chunks.text: SEC. 6. Minimum Age of Criminal Responsibility. [AMENDED BY RA 10630 SEC. 3 — see ra10630.txt] Original text: A child fifteen (15) years of age or under at the time of the commission of the offense shall be exempt from criminal liability. However, the child shall be subjected to an intervention program pursuant to Section 20 of this Act. A child above fifteen (15) years but below eighteen (18) years of age shall likewise be exempt from criminal liability and be subjected to an intervention program, unless he/she has acted with discernment, in which case, such child shall be subjected to the appropriate proceedings in accordance with this Act. The exemption from criminal liability herein established does not include exemption from civil liability, which shall be enforced in accordance with existing laws.

chunks.citation: RA 9344 (Juvenile Justice and Welfare Act of 2006), Sec. 7
chunks.text: SEC. 7. Determination of Age. - The child in conflict with the law shall enjoy the presumption of minority. He/She shall enjoy all the rights of a child in conflict with the law until proven to be eighteen (18) years old or older. Age may be determined from the child's birth certificate, baptismal certificate or any other pertinent documents; in the absence of these, from information given by the child, testimonies of others, physical appearance, and other relevant evidence. In case of doubt as to the age of the child, it shall be resolved in his/her favor.

chunks.citation: RA 9344 (Juvenile Justice and Welfare Act of 2006), Sec. 8
chunks.text: SEC. 8. Juvenile Justice and Welfare Council (JJWC). [AMENDED BY RA 10630 SEC. 4 — now under DSWD, not DOJ; see ra10630.txt]

chunks.citation: RA 9344 (Juvenile Justice and Welfare Act of 2006), Sec. 9
chunks.text: SEC. 9. Duties and Functions of the JJWC. [AMENDED BY RA 10630 SEC. 5 — see ra10630.txt]

chunks.citation: RA 9344 (Juvenile Justice and Welfare Act of 2006), Sec. 10
chunks.text: SEC. 10. Policies and Procedures on Juvenile Justice and Welfare. - All government agencies enumerated in Section 8 shall, with the assistance of the JJWC and within one (1) year from effectivity, draft policies and procedures consistent with the standards set in the law.

chunks.citation: RA 9344 (Juvenile Justice and Welfare Act of 2006), Sec. 11
chunks.text: SEC. 11. Child Rights Center (CRC). - The existing Child Rights Center of the Commission on Human Rights shall ensure that the status, rights and interests of children are upheld in accordance with the Constitution and international human rights instruments.

chunks.citation: RA 9344 (Juvenile Justice and Welfare Act of 2006), Sec. 12
chunks.text: SEC. 12. The Family. - The family shall be responsible for the primary nurturing and rearing of children which is critical in delinquency prevention. A child in conflict with the law shall be maintained in his/her family as far as practicable.

chunks.citation: RA 9344 (Juvenile Justice and Welfare Act of 2006), Sec. 13
chunks.text: SEC. 13. The Educational System. - Educational institutions shall work with families, community organizations and agencies in delinquency prevention and in rehabilitation/reintegration of children in conflict with the law, including alternative learning systems for those in custody.

chunks.citation: RA 9344 (Juvenile Justice and Welfare Act of 2006), Sec. 14
chunks.text: SEC. 14. The Role of the Mass Media. - The mass media shall promote child rights and delinquency prevention through balanced, non-sensationalized reporting. Undue, inappropriate publicity of a case involving a child in conflict with the law is a violation of the child's rights.

chunks.citation: RA 9344 (Juvenile Justice and Welfare Act of 2006), Sec. 15
chunks.text: SEC. 15. Establishment and Strengthening of Local Councils for the Protection of Children (LCPC). - LCPCs shall be established in all levels of local government to coordinate a comprehensive plan on delinquency prevention. One percent (1%) of barangay/municipal/city internal revenue allotment shall be allocated for LCPC programs.

chunks.citation: RA 9344 (Juvenile Justice and Welfare Act of 2006), Sec. 16
chunks.text: SEC. 16. Appointment of Local Social Welfare and Development Officer. - All LGUs shall appoint a duly licensed social worker as its local social welfare and development officer (LSWDO) tasked to assist children in conflict with the law.

chunks.citation: RA 9344 (Juvenile Justice and Welfare Act of 2006), Sec. 17
chunks.text: SEC. 17. The Sangguniang Kabataan. - The SK shall coordinate with the LCPC in formulating and implementing juvenile intervention and diversion programs in the community.

chunks.citation: RA 9344 (Juvenile Justice and Welfare Act of 2006), Sec. 18
chunks.text: SEC. 18. Development of a Comprehensive Juvenile Intervention Program. - A comprehensive juvenile intervention program covering at least a 3-year period shall be instituted in LGUs from barangay to provincial level, with an annual budget set aside for it.

chunks.citation: RA 9344 (Juvenile Justice and Welfare Act of 2006), Sec. 19
chunks.text: SEC. 19. Community-based Programs on Juvenile Justice and Welfare. - Instituted by LGUs through the LCPC, schools, youth organizations, consisting of three levels: (a) Primary intervention — general measures promoting social justice and equal opportunity; (b) Secondary intervention — measures to assist children at risk; (c) Tertiary intervention — measures to avoid unnecessary contact with the formal justice system and prevent re-offending.

chunks.citation: RA 9344 (Juvenile Justice and Welfare Act of 2006), Sec. 20
chunks.text: SEC. 20. Children Below the Age of Criminal Responsibility. [AMENDED BY RA 10630 SEC. 6 — see ra10630.txt]

chunks.citation: RA 9344 (Juvenile Justice and Welfare Act of 2006), Sec. 21
chunks.text: SEC. 21. Procedure for Taking the Child into Custody. - From the moment a child is taken into custody, the law enforcement officer shall: (a) explain in simple language/dialect why the child is in custody and the alleged offense; (b) inform the child of the reason for custody and his/her constitutional rights in an understandable language/dialect; (c) properly identify himself/herself; (d) refrain from vulgar/profane language or sexual harassment/abuse; (e) avoid displaying/using firearms, weapons, handcuffs or restraints unless absolutely necessary; (f) refrain from greater restraint than necessary; (g) avoid violence or unnecessary force; (h) determine the age of the child per Section 7; (i) within eight (8) hours of apprehension, turn over custody of the child to the Social Welfare and Development Office or accredited NGO, and notify the child's apprehension; (j) take the child immediately for physical and mental examination, kept confidential; (k) ensure detention quarters, if necessary, are separate from the opposite sex and from adult offenders; (l) record whether restraints were used and why, that parents/guardian/DSWD/PAO were informed, and the age-determination measures taken; (m) ensure all statements signed by the child are witnessed by parent/guardian, social worker, or legal counsel. A child shall only be searched by a law enforcement officer of the same gender and shall not be locked up in a detention cell.

chunks.citation: RA 9344 (Juvenile Justice and Welfare Act of 2006), Sec. 22
chunks.text: SEC. 22. Duties During Initial Investigation. [AMENDED BY RA 10630 SEC. 7 — see ra10630.txt]

chunks.citation: RA 9344 (Juvenile Justice and Welfare Act of 2006), Sec. 23
chunks.text: SEC. 23. System of Diversion. - Children in conflict with the law shall undergo diversion programs without court proceedings, subject to conditions: (a) where imposable penalty is not more than six (6) years imprisonment, the law enforcement officer or Punong Barangay with the LSWDO/LCPC shall conduct mediation, family conferencing and conciliation, with the child and family present; (b) in victimless crimes with imposable penalty not more than six (6) years, the LSWDO meets with the child and parents/guardians to develop the diversion/rehabilitation program with the BCPC; (c) where imposable penalty exceeds six (6) years, diversion measures may be resorted to only by the court.

chunks.citation: RA 9344 (Juvenile Justice and Welfare Act of 2006), Sec. 24
chunks.text: SEC. 24. Stages Where Diversion May be Conducted. - Diversion may be conducted at the Katarungang Pambarangay, police investigation, inquest or preliminary investigation stage, and at all levels/phases including judicial level.

chunks.citation: RA 9344 (Juvenile Justice and Welfare Act of 2006), Sec. 25
chunks.text: SEC. 25. Conferencing, Mediation and Conciliation. - A child in conflict with the law may undergo conferencing, mediation or conciliation outside the criminal justice system or prior to entry into it. A contract of diversion may be entered into during these proceedings.

chunks.citation: RA 9344 (Juvenile Justice and Welfare Act of 2006), Sec. 26
chunks.text: SEC. 26. Contract of Diversion. - If the child voluntarily admits the act during conferencing/mediation/conciliation, a diversion program shall be developed. This admission shall not be used against the child in subsequent proceedings. The diversion program is effective and binding once accepted in writing by the parties. The LSWDO supervises implementation. Diversion proceedings shall be completed within forty-five (45) days (period of prescription of offense suspended accordingly, not exceeding 45 days for this step and not exceeding 2 years overall for effectivity of a diversion program). The child must report monthly for evaluation. Failure to comply with the contract of diversion, as certified by the LSWDO, gives the offended party the option to institute appropriate legal action.

chunks.citation: RA 9344 (Juvenile Justice and Welfare Act of 2006), Sec. 27
chunks.text: SEC. 27. Duty of the Punong Barangay When There is No Diversion. - If diversion doesn't apply or isn't consented to, within three (3) days the Punong Barangay forwards the case records to the law enforcement officer, prosecutor, or appropriate court.

chunks.citation: RA 9344 (Juvenile Justice and Welfare Act of 2006), Sec. 28
chunks.text: SEC. 28. Duty of the Law Enforcement Officer When There is No Diversion. - Similarly, the Women and Children Protection Desk of the PNP or other officer handling the case forwards records to the prosecutor/judge for inquest/preliminary investigation. Documents transmitting the records must display the word "CHILD" in bold letters.

chunks.citation: RA 9344 (Juvenile Justice and Welfare Act of 2006), Sec. 29
chunks.text: SEC. 29. Factors in Determining Diversion Program. - (a) nature/circumstances of the offense; (b) frequency/severity of the act; (c) circumstances of the child (age, maturity, intelligence); (d) influence of family/environment; (e) reparation of injury to victim; (f) weight of evidence; (g) safety of the community; (h) best interest of the child.

chunks.citation: RA 9344 (Juvenile Justice and Welfare Act of 2006), Sec. 30
chunks.text: SEC. 30. Formulation of the Diversion Program. - Individualized treatment based on: (a) the child's feelings of remorse; (b) parents'/guardians' ability to guide and supervise; (c) victim's view on proposed measures; (d) availability of community-based rehabilitation programs.

chunks.citation: RA 9344 (Juvenile Justice and Welfare Act of 2006), Sec. 31
chunks.text: SEC. 31. Kinds of Diversion Programs. - At the level of the Punong Barangay: restitution of property, reparation of damage, indemnification for consequential damages, written/oral apology, care/guidance/supervision orders, counseling, attendance in trainings/seminars on anger management/conflict resolution/values formation and other skills, participation in community-based programs including community service, or participation in education/vocation/life skills programs. At the level of law enforcement officer/prosecutor: the above plus confiscation/forfeiture of proceeds or instruments of the crime. At the level of the appropriate court: the above plus written/oral reprimand or citation, fine, payment of cost of proceedings, or institutional care and custody.

chunks.citation: RA 9344 (Juvenile Justice and Welfare Act of 2006), Sec. 32
chunks.text: SEC. 32. Duty of the Prosecutor's Office. - There shall be a specially trained prosecutor to conduct inquest, preliminary investigation, and prosecution of cases involving a child in conflict with the law. Allegations of torture or ill-treatment during arrest/detention must be investigated by the prosecutor.

chunks.citation: RA 9344 (Juvenile Justice and Welfare Act of 2006), Sec. 33
chunks.text: SEC. 33. Preliminary Investigation and Filing of Information. [AMENDED BY RA 10630 SEC. 8 — see ra10630.txt]

chunks.citation: RA 9344 (Juvenile Justice and Welfare Act of 2006), Sec. 34
chunks.text: SEC. 34. Bail. - For purposes of recommending the amount of bail, the privileged mitigating circumstance of minority shall be considered.

chunks.citation: RA 9344 (Juvenile Justice and Welfare Act of 2006), Sec. 35
chunks.text: SEC. 35. Release on Recognizance. - Where a child is detained, the court shall order: (a) release on recognizance to parents/other suitable person; (b) release on bail; or (c) transfer to a youth detention home/rehabilitation center. The court shall not order detention of a child in a jail pending trial or hearing.

chunks.citation: RA 9344 (Juvenile Justice and Welfare Act of 2006), Sec. 36
chunks.text: SEC. 36. Detention of the Child Pending Trial. - Detention pending trial should be replaced by alternative measures (close supervision, intensive care, placement with family) whenever possible, and used only as a measure of last resort for the shortest possible time. Whenever detention is necessary, the child is detained in youth detention homes established by LGUs. In their absence, the child may be committed to DSWD or a recognized local rehabilitation center.

chunks.citation: RA 9344 (Juvenile Justice and Welfare Act of 2006), Sec. 37
chunks.text: SEC. 37. Diversion Measures. - Where the maximum penalty for the offense charged is imprisonment of not more than twelve (12) years (regardless of fine, or fine alone regardless of amount), and before arraignment, the court shall determine whether diversion is appropriate.

chunks.citation: RA 9344 (Juvenile Justice and Welfare Act of 2006), Sec. 38
chunks.text: SEC. 38. Automatic Suspension of Sentence. - Once a child under eighteen (18) at the time of the offense is found guilty, instead of pronouncing judgment of conviction, the court places the child under suspended sentence without need of application — even applicable if the child is already eighteen (18) or more at the time of pronouncement of guilt. The court imposes appropriate disposition measures per the Supreme Court Rule on Juveniles in Conflict with the Law.

chunks.citation: RA 9344 (Juvenile Justice and Welfare Act of 2006), Sec. 39
chunks.text: SEC. 39. Discharge of the Child in Conflict with the Law. - Upon recommendation of the social worker with custody of the child, the court dismisses the case and finally discharges the child once it finds the objectives of the disposition measures fulfilled. Discharge does not affect civil liability.

chunks.citation: RA 9344 (Juvenile Justice and Welfare Act of 2006), Sec. 40
chunks.text: SEC. 40. Return of the Child in Conflict with the Law to Court. - If disposition measures' objectives are not fulfilled or the child willfully fails to comply, the child is brought before the court for execution of judgment. If the child reaches eighteen (18) while under suspended sentence, the court determines whether to discharge, order execution of sentence, or extend the suspended sentence up to age twenty-one (21).

chunks.citation: RA 9344 (Juvenile Justice and Welfare Act of 2006), Sec. 41
chunks.text: SEC. 41. Credit in Service of Sentence. - The child is credited with the full time spent in actual commitment/detention under this Act.

chunks.citation: RA 9344 (Juvenile Justice and Welfare Act of 2006), Sec. 42
chunks.text: SEC. 42. Probation as an Alternative to Imprisonment. - The court may, after convicting and sentencing a child, place the child on probation in lieu of serving the sentence, taking into account the child's best interest.

chunks.citation: RA 9344 (Juvenile Justice and Welfare Act of 2006), Sec. 43
chunks.text: SEC. 43. Confidentiality of Records and Proceedings. - All records and proceedings involving a child in conflict with the law, from initial contact until final disposition, are privileged and confidential. Public is excluded during proceedings; records are not disclosed except to determine suspension of sentence/probation eligibility or enforce civil liability. Authorities must protect confidentiality, including maintaining a separate police blotter and a coding system to conceal identity. A child's records shall not be used in subsequent proceedings for the same offender as an adult, except when beneficial to the offender and with written consent. A former child in conflict with the law cannot be held guilty of perjury/concealment for not disclosing the case.

chunks.citation: RA 9344 (Juvenile Justice and Welfare Act of 2006), Sec. 44
chunks.text: SEC. 44. Objective of Rehabilitation and Reintegration. - To provide interventions/approaches/strategies enabling improved social functioning, with the end goal of reintegration to family and community as productive members.

chunks.citation: RA 9344 (Juvenile Justice and Welfare Act of 2006), Sec. 45
chunks.text: SEC. 45. Court Order Required. - No child shall be received in any rehabilitation/training facility without a valid court order after a hearing.

chunks.citation: RA 9344 (Juvenile Justice and Welfare Act of 2006), Sec. 46
chunks.text: SEC. 46. Separate Facilities from Adults. - Mandatory separation of children from adults in all rehabilitation/training facilities, unless members of the same family. No exceptions otherwise.

chunks.citation: RA 9344 (Juvenile Justice and Welfare Act of 2006), Sec. 47
chunks.text: SEC. 47. Female Children. - Female children in conflict with the law placed in an institution receive special attention, handled by female doctors/correction officers/social workers, accommodated separately from male children.

chunks.citation: RA 9344 (Juvenile Justice and Welfare Act of 2006), Sec. 48
chunks.text: SEC. 48. Gender-Sensitivity Training. - No personnel of rehabilitation/training facilities may handle children in conflict with the law without gender sensitivity training.

chunks.citation: RA 9344 (Juvenile Justice and Welfare Act of 2006), Sec. 49
chunks.text: SEC. 49. Establishment of Youth Detention Homes. [AMENDED BY RA 10630 SEC. 9 — retitled "Bahay Pag-asa"; see ra10630.txt]

chunks.citation: RA 9344 (Juvenile Justice and Welfare Act of 2006), Sec. 50
chunks.text: SEC. 50. Care and Maintenance of the Child in Conflict with the Law. [PARTIALLY AMENDED BY RA 10630 SEC. 10 — see ra10630.txt]

chunks.citation: RA 9344 (Juvenile Justice and Welfare Act of 2006), Sec. 51
chunks.text: SEC. 51. Confinement of Convicted Children in Agricultural Camps and other Training Facilities. - A child may, after conviction and upon court order, serve sentence in an agricultural camp/training facility maintained by BUCOR in coordination with DSWD, in lieu of a regular penal institution.

chunks.citation: RA 9344 (Juvenile Justice and Welfare Act of 2006), Sec. 52
chunks.text: SEC. 52. Rehabilitation of Children in Conflict with the Law. - Children whose sentences are suspended may undergo disposition measures suited to rehabilitation, including community-based programs: competency/life skills development, socio-cultural/recreational activities, community volunteer projects, leadership training, social services, homelife services, health services, spiritual enrichment, and community/family welfare services.

chunks.citation: RA 9344 (Juvenile Justice and Welfare Act of 2006), Sec. 53
chunks.text: SEC. 53. Youth Rehabilitation Center. - Provides 24-hour group care, treatment, rehabilitation under trained staff in a structured therapeutic environment, with quarterly progress reports to the court. DSWD establishes youth rehabilitation centers in each region.

chunks.citation: RA 9344 (Juvenile Justice and Welfare Act of 2006), Sec. 54
chunks.text: SEC. 54. Objectives of Community Based Programs. - (a) prevent disruption of education/livelihood; (b) prevent separation from parents/guardians; (c) facilitate rehabilitation/mainstreaming with community support; (d) minimize stigma by preventing jail detention.

chunks.citation: RA 9344 (Juvenile Justice and Welfare Act of 2006), Sec. 55
chunks.text: SEC. 55. Criteria of Community-Based Programs. - Every LGU establishes community-based rehabilitation/reintegration programs meeting JJWC criteria, considering the program's purpose, need for consent of child/parents, and participation of child-centered agencies.

chunks.citation: RA 9344 (Juvenile Justice and Welfare Act of 2006), Sec. 56
chunks.text: SEC. 56. After-Care Support Services for Children in Conflict with the Law. - Children whose cases are dismissed due to good behavior receive after-care services (counseling, community-based services) from the LSWDO for at least six (6) months.

chunks.citation: RA 9344 (Juvenile Justice and Welfare Act of 2006), Sec. 57
chunks.text: SEC. 57. Status Offenses. [AMENDED BY RA 10630 SEC. 11 — adds SEC. 57-A on Violations of Local Ordinances; see ra10630.txt] Original text: Any conduct not considered an offense or not penalized if committed by an adult shall not be considered an offense and shall not be punished if committed by a child.

chunks.citation: RA 9344 (Juvenile Justice and Welfare Act of 2006), Sec. 58
chunks.text: SEC. 58. Offenses Not Applicable to Children. - Persons below eighteen (18) are exempt from prosecution for vagrancy/prostitution (RPC Sec. 202), mendicancy (PD 1563), and rugby-sniffing (PD 1619), being inconsistent with the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child. Such persons undergo appropriate counseling and treatment instead.

chunks.citation: RA 9344 (Juvenile Justice and Welfare Act of 2006), Sec. 59
chunks.text: SEC. 59. Exemption from the Application of Death Penalty. - No death penalty shall be imposed on children in conflict with the law, notwithstanding the RPC, RA 9165 (Comprehensive Dangerous Drugs Act), or other special laws.

chunks.citation: RA 9344 (Juvenile Justice and Welfare Act of 2006), Sec. 60
chunks.text: SEC. 60. Prohibition Against Labeling and Shaming. - Competent authorities must refrain from branding/labeling children as young criminals, juvenile delinquents, prostitutes, or any derogatory name, from the initial contact onward. No discriminatory remarks/practices based on class or ethnic origin.

chunks.citation: RA 9344 (Juvenile Justice and Welfare Act of 2006), Sec. 61
chunks.text: SEC. 61. Other Prohibited Acts. - Prohibited: (a) threats of any kind; (b) abusive/coercive/punitive measures (cursing, beating, stripping, solitary confinement); (c) degrading/inhuman/cruel punishment (head-shaving, corrosive substances, forced public humiliation); (d) compelling involuntary servitude in any form.

chunks.citation: RA 9344 (Juvenile Justice and Welfare Act of 2006), Sec. 62
chunks.text: SEC. 62. Violation of the Provisions of this Act or Rules or Regulations in General. - Any person violating this Act or its IRR is punished, upon conviction, by a fine of P20,000–P50,000 or imprisonment of 8–10 years, or both, at the court's discretion, unless a higher penalty applies under the RPC or special laws. A public officer/employee is additionally held administratively liable with perpetual absolute disqualification.

chunks.citation: RA 9344 (Juvenile Justice and Welfare Act of 2006), Sec. 63
chunks.text: SEC. 63. Appropriations. [AMENDED BY RA 10630 SEC. 13 — see ra10630.txt]

chunks.citation: RA 9344 (Juvenile Justice and Welfare Act of 2006), Sec. 64
chunks.text: SEC. 64. Children in Conflict with the Law Fifteen (15) Years Old and Below. - Upon effectivity, cases of children 15 and below at the time of the offense are immediately dismissed and referred to the LSWDO for assessment. Those with suspended sentences undergoing rehabilitation are likewise released unless contrary to the child's best interest.

chunks.citation: RA 9344 (Juvenile Justice and Welfare Act of 2006), Sec. 65
chunks.text: SEC. 65. Children Detained Pending Trial. - The Family Court determines whether continued detention is necessary; if detained with adults, the court immediately orders transfer to a youth detention home.

chunks.citation: RA 9344 (Juvenile Justice and Welfare Act of 2006), Sec. 66
chunks.text: SEC. 66. Inventory of "Locked-up" and Detained Children in Conflict with the Law. - PNP, BJMP, and BUCOR submit an inventory of all children in conflict with the law under their custody to the JJWC within ninety (90) days of effectivity.

chunks.citation: RA 9344 (Juvenile Justice and Welfare Act of 2006), Sec. 67
chunks.text: SEC. 67. Children Who Reach the Age of Eighteen (18) Years Pending Diversion and Court Proceedings. - The appropriate diversion authority or Family Court determines the appropriate disposition; the child may apply for probation if qualified.

chunks.citation: RA 9344 (Juvenile Justice and Welfare Act of 2006), Sec. 68
chunks.text: SEC. 68. Children Who Have Been Convicted and are Serving Sentence. - Persons convicted and serving sentence who were minors at the time of the offense benefit retroactively from this Act; sentences adjusted accordingly; immediate release if qualified.

chunks.citation: RA 9344 (Juvenile Justice and Welfare Act of 2006), Sec. 69
chunks.text: SEC. 69. Rule Making Power. - The JJWC shall issue the IRRs within ninety (90) days from effectivity.

REPUBLIC ACT NO. 10630 — AN ACT STRENGTHENING THE JUVENILE JUSTICE SYSTEM IN THE PHILIPPINES, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 9344, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE "JUVENILE JUSTICE AND WELFARE ACT OF 2006" AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
Approved: October 3, 2013
(This law amends specific sections of RA 9344. Each section below states which RA 9344 section it amends and replaces.)

Section 1. The Title of Republic Act No. 9344 is hereby amended to read as follows: "An Act Establishing a Comprehensive Juvenile Justice and Welfare System, Creating the Juvenile Justice and Welfare Council under the Department of Social Welfare and Development, Appropriating Funds Therefor, and for Other Purposes."

Section 2. (amends RA 9344 SEC. 4, Definition of Terms — adds): "Bahay Pag-asa" refers to a 24-hour child-caring institution established, funded and managed by local government units (LGUs) and licensed and/or accredited nongovernment organizations (NGOs) providing short-term residential care for children in conflict with the law who are above fifteen (15) but below eighteen (18) years of age who are awaiting court disposition of their cases or transfer to other agencies or jurisdiction. Part of the features of a Bahay Pag-asa is an intensive juvenile intervention and support center (per Sections 20, 20-A and 20-B). A multi-disciplinary team composed of a social worker, a psychologist/mental health professional, a medical doctor, an educational/guidance counselor and a Barangay Council for the Protection of Children (BCPC) member shall operate the Bahay Pag-asa, working on the individualized intervention plan with the child and the child's family.

Section 3. (amends RA 9344 SEC. 6, Minimum Age of Criminal Responsibility — this is the current, controlling version): A child fifteen (15) years of age or under at the time of the commission of the offense shall be exempt from criminal liability. However, the child shall be subjected to an intervention program pursuant to Section 20 of this Act. A child is deemed to be fifteen (15) years of age on the day of the fifteenth anniversary of his/her birthdate. A child above fifteen (15) years but below eighteen (18) years of age shall likewise be exempt from criminal liability and be subjected to an intervention program, unless he/she has acted with discernment, in which case, such child shall be subjected to the appropriate proceedings in accordance with this Act. The exemption from criminal liability herein established does not include exemption from civil liability, which shall be enforced in accordance with existing laws.

Section 4. (amends RA 9344 SEC. 8, Juvenile Justice and Welfare Council — current, controlling version): The JJWC is created and attached to the Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD), placed under its administrative supervision (previously it was under the Department of Justice). Chaired by an Undersecretary of DSWD. Coordinates: DOJ, Council for the Welfare of Children (CWC), DepEd, DILG, Public Attorney's Office (PAO), Bureau of Corrections (BUCOR), Parole and Probation Administration (PPA), NBI, PNP, Bureau of Jail Management and Penology (BJMP), Commission on Human Rights (CHR), TESDA, National Youth Commission (NYC), and other juvenile justice institutions. Composed of representatives (rank not lower than director) from DOJ, DSWD, CWC, DepEd, DILG, CHR, NYC, two NGO representatives, DOH, and one representative each from the Leagues of Provinces, Cities, Municipalities and Barangays. A Regional Juvenile Justice and Welfare Committee (RJJWC) exists in each region, chaired by the DSWD regional director, ensuring implementation at the regional/LGU level, composed of similar member-agency representatives at the regional level.

Section 5. (amends RA 9344 SEC. 9, Duties and Functions of the JJWC — current version; also adds SEC. 9-A, Duties and Functions of the RJJWC): JJWC duties: oversee implementation of the Act; advise the President on juvenile justice policy; assist agencies in policy formulation; develop a 3-to-5-year national juvenile intervention program; coordinate intervention programs nationally; consult local government leagues; formulate policies with children's participation for delinquency prevention and CICL rehabilitation; collect data and conduct research on juvenile justice trends and needs; submit an annual report to Congress; ensure children's involvement in research/policy; conduct regular and spot inspections of detention/rehabilitation facilities; coordinate personnel training; submit an annual report to the President. RJJWC duties (SEC. 9-A) mirror these at the regional/LGU level: oversee regional implementation, assist in policy compliance, develop the regional 3-to-5-year juvenile intervention program, coordinate regional programs, oversee the region's Intensive Juvenile Intervention and Support Center, collect regional data, conduct regional facility inspections, coordinate regional trainings, and report annually to the JJWC.

Section 6. (amends RA 9344 SEC. 20, and adds SEC. 20-A, 20-B, 20-C, 20-D, 20-E — these are the current, controlling provisions for how children below/around the age of criminal responsibility are handled):

SEC. 20. Children Below the Age of Criminal Responsibility. — If the child taken into custody is fifteen (15) years old or below, the authority with initial contact, in consultation with the local social welfare and development officer (LSWDO), must immediately release the child to the custody of parents/guardian, or in their absence, the nearest relative. The child undergoes a community-based intervention program supervised by the LSWDO, unless the child's best interest requires referral to a youth care facility or Bahay Pag-asa managed by LGUs or licensed/accredited NGOs monitored by DSWD. The LSWDO determines appropriate programs in consultation with the child and custodian. If parents/guardians/nearest relatives cannot be located or refuse custody, the child may be released to: (a) a duly registered NGO or religious organization; (b) a barangay official or BCPC member; (c) the LSWDO or DSWD. If found dependent, abandoned, neglected or abused, and placement in a youth care facility/Bahay Pag-asa is in the child's best interest, the parents/guardians execute a written authorization for voluntary commitment; if unable/refusing, DSWD/LSWDO files a petition for involuntary commitment under PD 603. The minimum age for commitment to a youth care facility/Bahay Pag-asa is twelve (12) years old.

SEC. 20-A. Serious Crimes Committed by Children Who Are Exempt From Criminal Responsibility. — A child above twelve (12) up to fifteen (15) years of age who commits parricide, murder, infanticide, kidnapping and serious illegal detention where the victim is killed or raped, robbery with homicide or rape, destructive arson, rape, carnapping where the driver/occupant is killed or raped, or drug offenses under RA 9165 punishable by more than twelve (12) years imprisonment, is deemed a neglected child under PD 603 and mandatorily placed in the Intensive Juvenile Intervention and Support Center (IJISC) within a Bahay Pag-asa. The LSWDO (or DSWD social worker in their absence) files a petition for involuntary commitment within twenty-four (24) hours of the report. The court decides on the petition within seventy-two (72) hours of filing, and determines an initial placement period of at least one (1) year, based on reports from the IJISC's multi-disciplinary team.

SEC. 20-B. Repetition of Offenses. — A child above twelve (12) up to fifteen (15) who commits an offense a second time or more, having previously undergone a community-based intervention program, is deemed a neglected child under PD 603 and undergoes an intensive intervention program supervised by the LSWDO; if the child's best interest requires Bahay Pag-asa placement, the same voluntary/involuntary commitment process under SEC. 20 applies.

SEC. 20-C. Exploitation of Children for Commission of Crimes. — Any person who uses, takes advantage of, or profits from a child in committing a crime, including abuse of authority or confidence to induce/threaten/instigate the crime, receives the maximum penalty prescribed by law for that crime.

SEC. 20-D. Joint Parental Responsibility. — The court may require parents of a CICL to undergo counseling or other intervention, based on recommendation of the IJISC multi-disciplinary team, LSWDO, or DSWD. "Parents" means biological parents, adoptive parents, or individuals with custody of the child. Parents are liable for damages unless they prove reasonable supervision and diligence to prevent the offense.

SEC. 20-E. Assistance to Victims of Offenses Committed by Children. — The victim and victim's family are provided appropriate assistance and psychological intervention by the LSWDO, DSWD, and other concerned agencies.

Section 7. (amends RA 9344 SEC. 22, Duties During Initial Investigation — current, controlling version): The law enforcement officer determines where the CICL's case should be referred. The child's statement is taken in the presence of: (1) the child's counsel of choice, or a PAO lawyer in their absence; (2) the child's parents, guardian, or nearest relative; and (3) the LSWDO. In the absence of the parents/guardian/relative and LSWDO, the investigation proceeds in the presence of an NGO representative, religious group, or BCPC member. The social worker conducts an initial assessment — using DSWD-developed discernment assessment tools — to determine appropriate interventions and whether the child acted with discernment (without prejudice to a later, more comprehensive case study report). The local social worker then: (a) proceeds under Section 20 if the child is 15 or below, or is 15–17 and acted WITHOUT discernment; or (b) if the child is 15–17 and acted WITH discernment, proceeds to diversion.

Section 8. (amends RA 9344 SEC. 33, Preliminary Investigation and Filing of Information — current version): The prosecutor conducts a preliminary investigation when: (a) the child doesn't qualify for diversion; (b) the child/parents/guardian don't agree to diversion; or (c) the prosecutor, considering the social worker's assessment, determines diversion isn't appropriate. Upon serving the subpoena and complaint affidavit, the prosecutor notifies PAO of the service and the child's personal information/place of detention. Upon finding probable cause, the information is filed before the Family Court within forty-five (45) days of the start of preliminary investigation, and must allege the child acted with discernment.

Section 9. (amends RA 9344 SEC. 49, retitles Youth Detention Homes to "Bahay Pag-asa" — current, controlling version): Each province and highly-urbanized city (LGU) is responsible for building, funding, and operating a Bahay Pag-asa within its jurisdiction, per DSWD standards adopted by the JJWC. Every Bahay Pag-asa has an Intensive Juvenile Intervention and Support Center (IJISC) for children under Sections 20, 20-A, 20-B, requiring a more intensive multi-disciplinary intervention program, with standards set by the JJWC in partnership with DSWD, DOH, DepEd, and DILG.

Section 10. (amends RA 9344 SEC. 50, Care and Maintenance of the Child in Conflict with the Law — adds): LGUs' expected expenditures on the local juvenile intervention program for children at risk and CICL shall be included in the LGU's annual budget. Highly-urbanized cities and provincial governments must include a separate budget for constructing/maintaining the Bahay Pag-asa, including the IJISC's operation within it.

Section 11. (amends RA 9344 SEC. 57, Status Offenses — current version; adds SEC. 57-A): SEC. 57. Status Offenses. — Any conduct not considered an offense, or not penalized, if committed by an adult shall not be considered an offense and shall not be punished if committed by a child. SEC. 57-A. Violations of Local Ordinances. — Local ordinances on juvenile status offenses (curfew violations, truancy, parental disobedience, anti-smoking and anti-drinking laws) and light offenses/misdemeanors against public order or safety (disorderly conduct, public scandal, harassment, drunkenness, public intoxication, criminal nuisance, vandalism, gambling, mendicancy, littering, public urination, trespassing) are for the protection of children. No penalty is imposed on children for these violations — instead they are brought to their residence or to a barangay official at the barangay hall, released to the custody of parents. Appropriate intervention programs (counseling, group activities for children, parenting seminars for parents) must be provided in such ordinances. The child is recorded as a "child at risk," NOT as a "child in conflict with the law."

Section 12. (new — Mandatory Registry of Children in Conflict with the Law): All duty-bearers (barangay/BCPC workers, law enforcers, teachers, guidance counselors, social workers, prosecutors) who receive, handle, or refer CICL cases must faithfully record all pertinent information (age, residence, gender, crime, and details of the intervention/diversion undergone) to guarantee correct application of the law. The JJWC leads establishment of a centralized information management system on CICL.

Section 13. (amends RA 9344 SEC. 63, Appropriations — current version): Funding is charged against the JJWC's current-year appropriations under the DOJ budget; thereafter included in DSWD's annual budget under the General Appropriations Act. Four hundred million pesos (P400,000,000.00) is appropriated for constructing Bahay Pag-asa rehabilitation centers in high-CICL-incidence provinces/cities, identified by DSWD and JJWC, coursed through DPWH. LGUs provide a counterpart share of five million pesos (P5,000,000.00) per rehabilitation center.
Section 14. Implementing Rules and Regulations. — The JJWC promulgates the necessary IRR within sixty (60) days of this Act's effectivity. (This is the Revised IRR document — see irr_9344_10630.txt.)
Section 15. Separability Clause. — If any provision is held unconstitutional, other unaffected provisions remain valid and binding.
Section 16. Repealing Clause. — All inconsistent laws, decrees, ordinances and rules are modified or repealed accordingly.

Section 17. Effectivity Clause. — This Act took effect fifteen (15) days after publication in the Official Gazette or in at least two (2) national newspapers of general circulation (approved October 3, 2013).

COUNCIL RESOLUTION NO. 2
Series of 2014
SUBJECT: Revised Rules and Regulations Implementing Republic Act No.
9344, as amended by R.A. 10630
The Juvenile Justice and Welfare Council, pursuant to Section 69 of Republic Act No.
9344, the Juvenile Justice and Welfare Act of 2006 and Section 14 of Republic Act
10630 or “An Act Strengthening The Juvenile Justice System in the Philippines,
Amending for the Purpose Republic Act No. 9344,” promulgates the following
implementing rules and regulations:
PART I. GENERAL PROVISIONS

RULE 1. Title
These Rules shall be known and cited as the “Revised Rules and Regulations
Implementing Republic Act No. 9344, as amended by R.A. 10630” (the “Rules”).
These Rules are promulgated to prescribe the procedures and guidelines for the
implementation of the Act.

RULE 2. Definition of Terms
As used in these Rules, the term/s:
(1) “Act” refers to Republic Act No. 9344, as amended by Republic Act No.
10630.
(2) “Bahay Pag-asa” – refers to a 24-hour child-caring institution established,
funded and managed by local government units (LGUs) and licensed and/or
accredited non-government organizations (NGOs), providing short-term
residential care for children in conflict with the law, who are above fifteen (15)
but below eighteen (18) years of age, and who are awaiting court disposition
of their cases or transfer to other agencies or jurisdiction.
Part of the features of a “Bahay Pag-asa” is an Intensive Juvenile Intervention
and Support Center. This will cater to children in conflict with the law in
accordance with Sections 20, 20-A and 20-B of the Act.
A Multi-Disciplinary Team (MDT) composed of a Social Worker, a
psychologist/mental health professional, a medical doctor, an
educational/guidance counselor and a member of the Barangay Council for
the Protection of Children (BCPC), shall operate the “Bahay Pag-asa.” The
MDT will work on the individualized intervention plan with the child and the
child’s family.
(3) “Bail” refers to the security given for the release of the person in custody of
the law, furnished by a bondsman or a bonding company, to guarantee the
appearance of the person before any Court.
(4) “Best interest of the child” refers to the totality of circumstances and
conditions that are most beneficial for the survival, protection and feelings of
security of the child, and most likely to promote the child’s physical,
psychological and emotional development. It also means the least detrimental
| Pa ge

available alternative for safeguarding the growth and development of the
child.
(5) “Child” refers to a person under the age of eighteen (18) years.
(6) “Child who is above twelve (12) years of age” refers to a child who is at least
twelve (12) years and one (1) day old.
(7) “Child who is above fifteen (15) years of age” refers to a child who is at least
fifteen (15) years and one (1) day old.
(8) “Children-at-risk” or “CAR” refers to children who are vulnerable or at-risk of
behaving in a way that can harm themselves or others, or vulnerable and at
risk of being pushed and exploited to come into conflict with the law because
of personal, family and social circumstances, such as, but not limited to, the
following:
a. being abused by any person through sexual, physical, psychological,
mental, economic or any other means, and the parents or guardians
refuse, are unwilling, or unable to provide protection for the child;
b. being exploited sexually or economically;
c. being abandoned or neglected, and after diligent search and inquiry, the
parents or guardians cannot be found;
d. coming from a dysfunctional or broken family or being without a parent
or guardian;
e. being out of school;
f. being a street child;
g. being a member of a gang;
h. living in a community with a high level of criminality or drug abuse; and
i. living in situations of armed conflict.
Children-at-Risk also includes those children who violate the ordinances
enacted by local governments, concerning juvenile status offenses
enumerated in Section 57-A of the Act, such as, but not limited to, curfew
violations, truancy, parental disobedience, anti-smoking and anti-drinking
laws, as well as light offenses and misdemeanors against public order or
safety such as, but not limited to, disorderly conduct, public scandal,
harassment, drunkenness, public intoxication, criminal nuisance, vandalism,
gambling, mendicancy, littering, public urination, and trespassing. The
enactment of ordinances providing for juvenile status offenses by local
government units (LGUs) shall primarily promote greater protection for
children, by identifying children-at-risk, and not for purposes of employing
enforcement or punitive action.
Children-at-Risk also includes those who commit any of the following:
(1) Status offenses under Section 57 of the Act;
(2) Prostitution under Section 202 of the Revised Penal Code, as
amended;
(3) Mendicancy under Presidential Decree No. 1563; and
(4) Sniffing of rugby under Presidential Decree No. 1619.
The JJWC shall, from time to time, issue resolutions identifying other
offenses for which a child shall be considered as a child-at-risk and not a
child in conflict with the law.
(9) “Child in conflict with the law” or “CICL” refers to a child who is alleged as,
accused of, or adjudged as, having committed an offense under Philippine
laws.
(10) “Community-based programs” refers to the programs provided in a
community setting, developed for purposes of intervention, diversion, and
| Pa ge

rehabilitation of the child in conflict with the law, which are intended for the
purpose of reintegrating the child into the family and/or community.
(11) “Court” refers to a Family Court, or in places where there are no Family
Courts, any Regional Trial Court.
(12) “Deprivation of liberty” refers to any form of detention or imprisonment,
or to the placement of a child in conflict with the law in a public or private
custodial setting, from which the child in conflict with the law is not permitted
to leave at will, by order of any judicial or administrative authority.
(13) “Diversion” refers to an alternative, child-appropriate process of
determining the responsibility and treatment of a child in conflict with the law,
on the basis of the child’s social, cultural, economic, psychological or
educational background, without resorting to formal court proceedings
(14) “Diversion Program” refers to the program that the child in conflict with
the law is required to undergo after being found responsible for an offense,
without resorting to formal court proceedings.
(15) “Duty-bearer” shall refer to persons who are responsible for providing
care, addressing the needs and protecting the rights of a child within the
juvenile justice and welfare system.
(16) “Initial contact with the child” refers to the apprehension or taking into
custody of a child in conflict with the law by law enforcement officers or
private citizens. It includes the time when the child alleged to be in conflict
with the law receives a subpoena under Section 3(b) of Rule 112 of the
Revised Rules of Criminal Procedure or summons under Section 6(a) or
Section 9(b) of the same Rule, in cases that do not require preliminary
investigation or where there is no necessity to place the child alleged to be in
conflict with the law under immediate custody.
(17) “Intensive Juvenile Intervention and Support Center” or “IJISC” refers to
a special program or unit within the “Bahay Pag-asa” or any child-caring
facility of the DSWD or licensed and accredited NGOs, to address the needs
of the CICL for intensive intervention programs and services.
(18) “Intervention” generally refers to programmatic approaches or
systematic social protection programs for children that are designed and
intended to:
a. Promote the physical and social well-being of the children;
b. Avert or prevent juvenile delinquency from occurring; and
c. Stop or prevent children from re-offending.
(19) “Juvenile Justice and Welfare System” refers to a system of dealing
with children-at-risk and children in conflict with the law, which provides child-
appropriate proceedings, including programs and services for prevention,
diversion, rehabilitation, reintegration and after-care to ensure the child’s
normal growth and development.
(20) “Offense” refers to any act or omission punishable under special penal
laws or the Revised Penal Code. For purposes of providing appropriate
services for children, the term ‘offense’ shall include violations of ordinances
of local government units.
(21) “Probation” refers to a disposition under which a defendant, after
conviction and sentence, is released, subject to the conditions imposed by the
Court and the person is placed under the supervision of a probation officer.
(22) “Recognizance” refers to an undertaking, in lieu of a bail bond, assumed
by a parent or custodian, who shall be responsible for ensuring the
appearance in Court of the child in conflict with the law, whenever required.
(23) “Referral” shall refer to a process where a duty-bearer, within the
juvenile justice and welfare system, endorses the CICL to the appropriate
service provider for appropriate care or intervention. ‘Referral’ includes the
endorsement of the victim for appropriate assistance and intervention.
| Pa ge

(24) “Victimless Crimes” refers to offenses where there is no private
offended party.

RULE 3. Construction
In case of doubt, the provisions of the Act and these Rules shall be construed liberally in
favor of the child in conflict with the law.
A liberal construction in favor of the child means that the interpretation is consistent with
the principle of the best interest and welfare of the child, the declared State Policy
embodied in Section 2 of the Act, the rights of the child in conflict with the law, and the
principles of restorative justice.

RULE 4. Declaration of State Policies
The following State policies shall be observed at all times:
(1) The State recognizes the vital role of children and youth in nation-building and
shall promote and protect their physical, moral, spiritual, intellectual and social
well-being. It shall inculcate in the youth patriotism and nationalism, and
encourage their involvement in public and civic affairs.
(2) The State shall protect the best interests of the child, through measures that will
ensure the observance of international standards of child protection, especially
those to which the Philippines is a Party. The conduct of all proceedings before
any authority shall be consistent with the best interest of the child, and shall allow
the child to participate and to express himself or herself freely. The concerned
government agency shall ensure the participation of children in the program,
policy formulation and implementation related to juvenile justice and welfare.
(3) The State likewise recognizes the right of children to assistance, including proper
care and nutrition, and special protection from all forms of neglect, abuse, cruelty
and exploitation, and other conditions prejudicial to their normal development.
(4) Pursuant to Article 40 of the United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child,
the State recognizes the right of every child alleged as, accused of, adjudged, or
recognized as having infringed the penal law to be treated in a manner consistent
with the promotion of the child’s sense of dignity and worth, taking into account
the child’s age and desirability of promoting the child’s reintegration. Whenever
appropriate and desirable, the State shall adopt measures for dealing with such
children without resorting to judicial proceedings, and guarantee that human
rights and legal safeguards are fully respected. It shall ensure that children are
dealt with in a manner appropriate to their well-being, by providing for, among
others, a variety of disposition measures such as care, guidance and supervision
orders, counseling, probation, foster care, education and vocational training
programs and other alternatives to institutional care.
(5) The administration of the juvenile justice and welfare system shall take into
consideration the cultural and religious perspectives of the Filipino people,
particularly the indigenous peoples and the Muslims, consistent with the
protection of the rights of children belonging to these communities.
(6) The State shall apply and operationalize the principles of restorative justice in all
its laws, policies and programs applicable to children in conflict with the law.
(7) Institutionalizing a child is a measure of last resort. It is only allowed if it is for the
best interest of the child, and should only be done for the shortest possible period
of time.
(8) The “Bahay Pag-Asa” or Youth Rehabilitation Centers shall always be gender-
sensitive and child-friendly in its design, space and programs.
| Pa ge

RULE 5. Application of the Principle of Restorative Justice
In repairing the harm done by a CICL, the agencies shall exert all efforts to apply the
Principle of Restorative Justice.
Restorative justice refers to a principle that requires a process of resolving conflicts with
the maximum involvement of the victim, the offender, their families and the community.
Among others, it seeks to achieve the following goals:
(1) Reparation for the victim;
(2) Reconciliation of the offender, the offended and the community;
(3) Reassurance to the offender that he or she can be reintegrated into society; and
(4) Enhancement of public safety by activating the offender, the victim and the
community in prevention strategies and programs.
Implementers and duty-bearers shall ensure that the victims and their families are
properly cared for and their needs are properly addressed. The assistance shall not be
limited to legal assistance and psycho-social intervention by the appropriate agencies.
The JJWC, through the concerned agencies, shall issue the appropriate guidelines for
the provision of assistance and intervention to victims and their families, as well as for
their proper referral.

RULE 6. Children of Indigenous Cultural Communities/Indigenous Peoples (ICCs/IPs)
Consistent with Section 15 of Republic Act No. 8371, or “The Indigenous Peoples’
Rights Act of 1997,” ICCs/IPs shall, in dealing with children in conflict with the law, have
the right to use their own commonly-accepted justice systems, conflict resolution
institutions, peace-building processes or mechanisms, and other customary laws and
practices, within their respective communities, as may be compatible with the national
legal system and with internationally-recognized human rights.

Rule 7. a. Right to Confidentiality and Privacy
The right to privacy of a child in conflict with the law shall be respected at all stages of
the proceedings. As such, all records and proceedings involving children in conflict with
the law, from initial contact until the final disposition of the case, shall be considered
privileged and confidential.
The public shall be excluded during the proceedings, and the records shall not be
disclosed directly or indirectly to anyone, by any of the parties or the participants in the
proceedings, for any purpose whatsoever, except to determine the application of a
suspended sentence, the grant of probation under the Probation Law, or to enforce the
civil liability imposed in the criminal action.
All concerned duty-bearers shall undertake all measures to protect the identity of the
child, and to uphold the confidentiality of the proceedings, including non-disclosure of
the records to the media, maintaining a separate police blotter for cases involving
children in conflict with the law, and adopting a system of coding to conceal material
information which will lead to the child’s identity. Records of a child in conflict with the
law shall not be used in subsequent proceedings for cases involving the same offender
as an adult, except when beneficial to the offender and upon the offender’s written
consent.
All duty-bearers shall enjoin the media practitioners to observe the guidelines and
protocols related to reporting and coverage of cases involving children, particularly the
| Pa ge

Guide for Media Practitioners on the Reporting and Coverage of Case Involving
Children, as promulgated by the Committee for the Special Protection of Children.

RULE 8. Rights of the Child in Conflict with the Law
Every child in conflict with the law shall have the following rights, including but not
limited to:
(a) The right not to be subjected to torture or other cruel, inhuman or degrading
treatment or punishment;
(b) The right not to be imposed upon a sentence of capital punishment or life
imprisonment, without the possibility of release;
(c) The right not to be deprived, unlawfully or arbitrarily of his or her liberty;
detention or imprisonment being a disposition of last resort, and which shall
be for the shortest appropriate period of time;
(d) The right to be treated with humanity and respect for the inherent dignity of
the person, and in a manner which takes into account the needs of a person
appropriate to their age. In particular, a child deprived of liberty shall be
separated from adult offenders at all times. No child shall be detained
together with adult offenders. The CICL shall be conveyed separately to or
from court. The CICL shall await hearing of his or her own case in a
separate holding area. A child in conflict with the law shall have the right to
maintain contact with his or her family through correspondence and visits,
save in exceptional circumstances;
| Pa ge

(e) The right to prompt access to legal and other appropriate assistance, as well
as the right to challenge the legality of the deprivation of liberty before a
Court or other competent, independent and impartial authority, and the right
to a prompt decision in such action;
(f) The right to bail and recognizance, in appropriate cases;
(g) The right to testify as a witness for his or her own behalf, under the Supreme
Court Rule on the Examination of a Child Witness;
(h) The right to privacy to be fully respected and protected at all stages of the
proceedings;
(i) The right to diversion, if the child is qualified and voluntarily avails of the
same;
(j) The right to receive judgment, where the penalty is proportionate to the
gravity of the offense, and where the CICL’s best interest, the rights of the
victim and the needs of society, are all taken into consideration by the Court,
consistent with the principle of restorative justice;
(k) The right to have restrictions on personal liberty limited to a minimum, and
where discretion is given by law to the Judge to determine whether to
impose a fine or a term of imprisonment, the imposition of a fine shall be

(n) The right to be free from liability for perjury, concealment or

(o) Other rights, as provided for under existing laws, rules and regulations.

RULE 15. Family

PART VI. INTERVENTION PROGRAMS

RULE 21. Definition of Intervention
“Intervention” generally refers to programmatic approaches or systematic social
protection programs for children that are designed to:
| P a ge

(1) Promote the physical and social well-being of children;
(2) Avert or prevent juvenile delinquency from occurring; and
(3) Stop or prevent children from re-offending.
“Intervention,” as used in these Rules, has three levels:
(1) Primary Intervention includes general measures to promote social justice and
equal opportunity, which tackle the perceived root causes of offending. These
shall include programs on advocacy, and socio-economic, health and nutrition,
training and education services.
(2) Secondary Intervention includes measures to assist children-at-risk, i.e., protective
services for children; and
(3) Tertiary Intervention includes measures to avoid unnecessary contact with the
formal justice system, and other measures to prevent re-offending, i.e., diversion
programs, rehabilitation, reintegration and after-care services, which shall be
further defined in PART IX, PART X and PART XIII of these Rules.
Intervention can be implemented in different settings, which may include, but not limited
to, the community, the school or the youth care facility.
Intervention shall include psycho-social intervention, which may be delivered through
center-based or community-based interventions.
All interventions shall include intervention undertaken with the family of the child.

Rule 22. b. Community Based Programs in the LGU
As provided for in Section 19 of the Act, the community-based programs for juvenile
intervention and delinquency prevention shall respond to the special needs, problems,
interests and concerns of children, and offer appropriate counseling and guidance to

All community-based programs to be designed by LGUs shall consist of the three levels,
as provided under Rule 23.

as amended. Thereafter, the Comprehensive National Juvenile Intervention Program

The CNJIP shall be developed, enhanced and reviewed with the participation of:

(2) Non-government organizations;
(3) Child and youth organizations; and
(4) The League of Provinces of the Philippines, League of Cities of the Philippines,

Rule 24. a. Development, Review and Enhancement of the CLJIP
